entities.summary:
Pope John IX was the bishop of Rome and ruler of the Papal States from January 898 to his death in 900. He played a crucial role in the politics of the time, navigating the complex web of alliances and rivalries between the Holy Roman Empire, the Frankish Kingdom, and the Carolingian dynasty. His leadership during this period had a lasting impact on the development of the Catholic Church and the politics of the medieval world.

Born in the late 9th century, John IX was chosen as pope in 898 after the death of Pope Formosus. He was elected by a group of cardinals who were opposed to the imperial candidate, leading to a significant power struggle between the papacy and the Holy Roman Empire.

One of John IX's most notable achievements was his involvement in the Treaty of St. Bavon, a peace agreement between the Holy Roman Empire and the Frankish Kingdom. This treaty marked a significant turning point in the history of the Holy Roman Empire, as it established a lasting peace between the two powers and paved the way for the rise of the Ottonian dynasty.

John IX's legacy as pope is complex and multifaceted. He was a strong advocate for the rights of the Catholic Church and played a key role in the development of the papacy as a major political power. However, his leadership was also marked by controversy and conflict, particularly with the Holy Roman Emperor Otto II.

Despite his controversies, John IX is remembered as a significant figure in the history of the Catholic Church and the medieval world. His leadership during this period had a lasting impact on the development of the Church and the politics of Europe, and he remains an important figure in the annals of papal history.
